primitives.verbatim_quote: While no report of such an experiment has been found, it seems reasonable to suppose on the analogy of the experiments of Gantt and Grindley that a food so adulterated would be less effective as a "primary" reinforcing agent than would an equal weight of the natural food.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core mathematical structure emerges from the interplay between reinforcement quantity (q), habit strength (m), and the F-constant that governs learning rate. The hypothesis posits that m varies with both q and the quality of the reinforcing agent, implying a dual dependency. The Gantt analogies suggest a saturating function where m increases with q but asymptotes at a physiological maximum. This leads to a functional form m(q) = F·q + C, where F is calibrated from experimental data and C represents baseline behavior. The breakdown regime occurs when q exceeds the saturation threshold, causing m to plateau. Adulteration introduces a scaling factor that reduces F, thereby lowering the effective m even for identical q. The dual nature of the system—quantity and quality—suggests a tensorial or multi-dimensional parameter space for m(q, quality). The curves in Figure 29 visualize this behavior, showing how different q-values produce distinct trajectories toward m_{\text{max}}. The implications extend to modeling learning policies in GSE, where optimal q must balance speed of acquisition against physiological limits.
